name: Onesiphorus
charge: Oft refreshing Paul, and not ashamed of his chain; seeking him out very diligently in Rome
summary: Writing from Rome while he waited on execution, Paul said that all they which are in Asia had turned away from him, and then named one house that had not: the house of Onesiphorus, who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chain, sought him out very diligently in Rome until he found him, and had ministered to him in many things at Ephesus (2 Timothy 1:15-18). Paul’s prayer over him is that the Lord give mercy to his house and that he find mercy of the Lord in that day, and at the close of the same letter he salutes that household again (2 Timothy 4:19).
offenseFull: Paul had already told Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony of the Lord nor of him, his prisoner, but to be partaker of the afflictions of the gospel (2 Timothy 1:8). Then he stated the plain case: all they which are in Asia be turned away from me, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them (2 Timothy 1:15). These were not strangers. Men who had stood strong in this gospel and warred alongside him had left him. The teaching refuses to soften it and applies it directly, because we have watched it happen: brothers and sisters we called friends, who broke bread with us, stayed in our homes, and knew our families, offended at the word and turned to tearing the work down. Christ had already said that many would be offended, and would betray one another and hate one another (Matthew 24:10).

Against all of Asia, one house. Paul asked the Lord to give mercy to the house of Onesiphorus, because he often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chain (2 Timothy 1:16). When he was in Rome he sought Paul out very diligently, and found him (2 Timothy 1:17). There were no phones and no addresses to call; a man looking for a prisoner in Rome had to go on foot and keep asking until somebody told him, and he did it knowing what the chain meant and knowing who would see him doing it. This was not a single gesture either, because Timothy knew very well in how many things the same man had ministered to Paul at Ephesus (2 Timothy 1:18). Christ counts a visit to a man in prison as done to himself, and sets it among the works that divide the sheep from the goats (Matthew 25:36-40). The command is to remember them that are in bonds as bound with them (Hebrews 13:3), and the Hebrews had already done it, becoming companions of them that were so used and taking the spoiling of their goods joyfully (Hebrews 10:33-34).
judgmentFull: Paul had nothing left to give him but a prayer, and he prayed it twice: mercy on his house, and that the man himself might find mercy of the Lord in that day (2 Timothy 1:16-18). That day is the day Paul had been reasoning about all through the letter. In that day the song is sung in the land of Judah, and the gates are opened that the righteous nation which keeps the truth may enter in (Isaiah 26:1-2). The truth there is the law, since his righteousness is an everlasting righteousness and his law is the truth (Psalms 119:142), and it is the keeping of the commandments that gives right to the tree of life

and entrance through the gates into the city (Revelation 22:14), the city with twelve gates and the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel written on them (Revelation 21:12). A man who was not ashamed of a prisoner’s chain in Rome is asking for mercy at the only bar that matters. At the end of the same letter, when almost everyone else had gone, Paul saluted the household of Onesiphorus by name (2 Timothy 4:19). That is the whole reward on record, and it is the one he asked for.

text.text: Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;
This thou knowest, that all they which are in Asia be turned away from me; of whom are Phygellus and Hermogenes.
The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain:
But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me.
The Lord grant unto him that he may find mercy of the Lord in that day: and in how many things he ministered unto me at Ephesus, thou knowest very well.
And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another.
Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink?
When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee?
Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee?
And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body.
Partly, whilst ye were made a gazingstock both by reproaches and afflictions; and partly, whilst ye became companions of them that were so used.
For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
In that day shall this song be sung in the land of Judah; We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks.
Open ye the gates, that the righteous nation which keepeth the truth may enter in.
Thy righteousness is an everlasting righteousness, and thy law is the truth.
Blessed are they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life, and may enter in through the gates into the city.
And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel:
Salute Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.
